spec.title: Reviewers state properties, not implementations; enforce where the schema can
spec.problem: Every agent may flag a defect; today every agent may also design the fix. On run #30 that produced two load-bearing PROPERTIES (SecOps: the tripwire's glob set must be a UNION with the built-in defaults so config can only ever widen the halt; DBA: strip only what every target dialect agrees is a comment, classify executable on divergence) and one IMPLEMENTATION (DBA shipped a five-line replacement for the `--` scanner). The implementation was correct and still harmful: a data-safety lens designed the fix for a module that serves several lenses, and Dev arbitrates between six proposed mechanisms instead of choosing one. PR #35's owner summary after a day of dogfooding 0.21.0 was "great at finding bugs, not great at preventing them / solving them quickly"; this targets the second half. The rule: every agent may flag an issue, identify a problem, or name a shortcoming, and must state what a correct fix would have to SATISFY; only QA and Dev may propose HOW, through the TDD contract. The issue's closing constraint is the hard part - "a rule stated only in agent prose is a norm, and this repo has measured what norms are worth" - and Phase 2 turned that constraint on this spec itself. Round 1 found the schema seat has a measured enforcement record of ZERO in this repository. Round 2 found WHY, and it is worse than a local quirk: the SubagentStop validator is inert in every PLUGIN-INSTALLED project, which is the shipping product's default deployment (filed as #66). The centre of gravity is therefore the honesty statement, and the honesty statement must be scoped by DEPLOYMENT MODE, not by repository.
spec.root_cause: There is no channel in the review artifact schemas for the one thing a reviewer is now required to produce. `review.schema.json` and `peer-review.schema.json` give a concern exactly three fields (severity, description, location) plus a free-text `notes`, so a property and a patch are the same field, and nothing distinguishes them. Worse, the schema and the SecOps contract actively invite the implementation: `review.schema.json` types a `vulnerabilities[].remediation` field, and `secops.md:29` instructs "when you veto, be specific about the remediation" with a shipped example at `secops.md:169` that names a specific middleware and a specific numeric limit ("Wrap with the global rate-limit middleware (10 req/min).").
requirements: R1. State the rule once, canonically, and place that statement in the shared Phase 4 preamble in `commands/pipeline.md` (owned section) AND in every agent definition under `agents/`. The formulation has THREE clauses, not one, because Phase 2 established that the first clause alone weakens the veto. (a) SCOPE: a reviewer may say anything about WHAT MUST BE TRUE and what that truth would COST; only QA and Dev may say HOW to make it true. (b) MEASURABILITY: a property that BINDS a downstream role carries, in itself, the OBSERVATION whose outcome decides whether it is met - an observation a reader other than its author can make, and that a defect can fail. (c) HALVES: where the property has two halves and one is cheap to satisfy, the property says in itself that satisfying only the cheap half approves the defect. Clauses (b) and (c) are `art-director.md:52` and `:53-54` lifted verbatim in force; R2's earlier draft cited that prior art while dropping both, and the measured consequence is that 'the token comparison must not be vulnerable to timing attacks' would have become a binding ask with no observation attached, which is weaker than the mechanism form it replaces. The passage must also reconcile the two rules it collides with: `pipeline.md:746` ("before you demand a guardrail, name the CORRECT work it refuses") reasons about a PROPERTY'S COST, and `evidence.md:278-280`'s ship-or-block line classifies the DEFECT'S REACHABILITY to decide whether the property binds now or is a note. Neither names a mechanism, so both stay in bounds with no carve-out.

R2. State TWO exemptions, because R1 alone forbids two things that must stay allowed. (a) CANDIDATE MECHANISM: a reviewer MAY reason about a candidate mechanism in order to test a property's cost or falsify its necessity - the preamble's guardrail-refuses rule requires exactly this. What it may not do is deposit that mechanism in the artifact as the ask; where the belief is worth recording it goes in a NON-BINDING field that no downstream role is obliged to act on (`art-director.md:52`'s `rationale_not_checked` is the prior art to generalize). (b) EXTERNALLY-FIXED VALUE: a value an authority OUTSIDE this reviewer fixed may be stated LITERALLY as a binding ask, with its source named so the claim is checkable. THE DISCRIMINATOR TURNS ON THE ASK'S FORM, NOT ON THE BOUND'S ORIGIN, and this is a correction of round 1's wording (SecOps supplied that wording and withdrew it in round 2, attributing the error to itself). The test, applied to the written ask alone: (i) does the ask BIND ON A LITERAL VALUE - a number, a version, a scheme name, a header token? If it does not - if it states a CONDITION together with the observation that decides it - it is in bounds whoever first thought of it, and its author's mental history is irrelevant and unobservable. If it does bind on a literal, (ii) is a checkable source for that literal named? Named source, in bounds; no named source, out of bounds. Provenance-of-a-LITERAL is observable in the artifact; provenance-of-a-JUDGEMENT is observable nowhere, and a criterion resting on the latter cannot be applied by anyone but its author, which is what R1(b) forbids. Worked, and all three must remain IN BOUNDS: "the rate limit must be low enough that credential stuffing is not economical, measured by <observation>"; "the token lifetime must be short enough that a leaked token expires before a human can act on it, measured by <observation>"; "the payload cap must be small enough that one request cannot exhaust the parser, measured by <observation>". These are the canonical R1-conformant form for the majority of security findings, which no statute backs. (c) THE EXEMPTION'S ILLUSTRATIONS MUST EXHIBIT BOTH SHAPES an externally-fixed value takes, because q3 ruled that the shipped EXAMPLE is what a reviewer copies. NUMERIC: a regulation's threshold, an interop contract's version floor, a named advisory's fixed version. IDENTIFIER, which is the shape SecOps states most often and which round 1's three-numeric illustration set did not exhibit at all: a provider's HMAC-SHA256 webhook signature scheme, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, PKCE `S256`. At least one shipped example must be an identifier. Exemption (a) does not cover (b): a statute-fixed bound is neither a candidate nor a belief, and routing it to a non-binding field converts a compliance requirement into advice.

R3. Give the property a typed home on the reviewer concern shape in BOTH `review.schema.json` (`definitions/agentBlock` concerns) and `peer-review.schema.json` (`definitions/panelVerdict` concerns), and make it MACHINE-REQUIRED where the schema can reach. SecOps's own artifact contract (`secops.md:156`) routes a finding into THREE arrays - `concerns`, `vulnerabilities`, `compliance_flags` - so the location set is derived from the contract, not from the subset that was measured. (a) `review.schema.json` `agentBlock` concerns.items.required gains the new field. (b) `review.schema.json` `#/properties/secops`'s `vulnerabilities[].items` gains a `required` list that includes the property-carrying field, because SecOps's contract instructs `concerns: []` when findings live elsewhere (`secops.md:156-171`), so a change that binds only on `concerns[]` binds everywhere except the role holding the veto. (c) `compliance_flags[].items` is NOT guarded by this change and must be NAMED as unreached under R5(a). MEASURED as landable: both (a) and (b) applied to a scratch copy leave the shipped validator self-test at 68 passed / 0 failed, and the four-cell fixture in measured_state shows a critical auth-bypass filed the way SecOps is contractually told to file it goes from SILENT PASS to `decision:block`. WHAT R3(b) BUYS, NARROWED TO WHAT WAS MEASURED (DBA D2): on the deployment where the gate fires, 29 of 29 already-written blocking-severity rows (3 critical, 26 high) ALREADY carry `remediation`, so the requirement costs the population its own rationale is about exactly nothing, and correspondingly guards nothing there today; the 17 rows it does newly bind are all non-blocking observations (info 9, low 4, medium 4) where 'there is nothing to remediate' is a legitimate state. The requirement is therefore BROADER than the rationale that justifies it, necessarily, because the walker cannot condition on severity, and R5(d) must say so and carry the count. Do NOT add the field to `peer-review.schema.json`'s `required` list this round; MEASURED as not landable (see out_of_scope). The implementation chooses the spelling and JSON type, and must state in each schema `description` what the field carries and what it must NOT carry.

R4. Do not close ANY item subschema this change gives a required list to. That is THREE subschemas, not two (DBA D3): `review.schema.json`'s `agentBlock` concerns.items, `peer-review.schema.json`'s `panelVerdict` concerns.items, and - added this round and previously unnamed - `review.schema.json` `#/properties/secops`'s `vulnerabilities.items`, which is the subschema an editor's hands are actually on. None may gain `additionalProperties: false`. This is not stylistic: the reversibility of the whole change rests on it. A shard written under the new contract validates cleanly against the CURRENT un-amended schemas precisely because the walker ignores undeclared keys, and all 13 archived blocks carry role-specific extra keys (`id`, `title`, `evidence`, `detail`, `ask`, `text`, `proposed_anchor`, `must_fix_before_merge`) that survive validation only for that reason; on the vulnerabilities side, 1 of 229 measured live rows carries undeclared keys (`resolved`, `resolution`) and would be stranded. Closing any of the three is a plausible tidying instinct for someone editing these exact lines and it converts a reversible additive field into a one-way migration that invalidates already-written instances at once. The invariant: an instance valid under either contract version remains valid under the other.

R5. Record the enforcement reality HONESTLY, and the honest statement is now materially harsher than round 2's, because round 2 named the cause. It must name SIX things, none of which may be omitted. (a) WHICH LOCATIONS THE REQUIREMENT REACHES AND WHICH IT DOES NOT, quantified over the arrays SecOps's own contract routes a blocking or veto finding into, which is THREE and not two: it blocks on Phase 2 `concerns[]`; it blocks on Phase 2 SecOps `vulnerabilities[]`; it does NOT reach Phase 2 SecOps `compliance_flags[]`, and it does NOT block on any Phase 4 `peer-review` artifact. The compliance channel is the one this change must name rather than guard, and it is the channel SecOps's veto protocol is contractually reserved for: `compliance_flags[].action`'s enum has `"block"` as its first member, and `compliance_flags.items` has NO `required` list at all, so - MEASURED through the shipped `hooks/subagent-stop.sh` against the doubly-mutated plugin copy, with the unmutated copy as the non-zero control - a SecOps VETO recorded as `{verdict: VETO, concerns: [], vulnerabilities: [], compliance_flags: [{}]}` validates SILENT, exit 0, with no statute, no concern and no action. Naming it as unreached satisfies the property at zero cost; guarding it is not asked for and is not this change's business. The statement quantifies over LOCATIONS a blocking finding can occupy, not over files, and the set is derived from `secops.md:156`'s artifact contract so that a fourth location added later is visibly missing rather than silently absent. (b) THE MEASURED ENFORCEMENT RECORD, SCOPED BY DEPLOYMENT MODE AND NOT BY REPOSITORY, CARRYING ITS WINDOW, ITS POPULATION AND ITS RE-DERIVATION. This is the correction that matters most in the whole spec, and round 2's draft got it wrong in the direction that would have shipped a warranty to readers it does not protect. THE RECORD: the shipped validator, replayed today, reports 17 schema violations across the 13 reviewer/panel blocks archived from runs #34 and #43, against rules in force since the first release commit; replaying #43's archived SecOps shard through the shipped `hooks/subagent-stop.sh` emits `decision:block` on all seven. THE SPLIT: across every Claude Code session on one machine (~/.claude/projects, 1638 transcript files / 353,907 lines, read 2026-08-21) the validator has emitted 56 genuine blocks, and every one of them is in a project that dispatches BARE agent names because the plugin is disabled there and its agents are local `.claude/agents/*.md` files. Across roughly 635 PLUGIN-NAMESPACED dispatches in six repositories - INCLUDING an adopting project with 365 of them - it has emitted ZERO. THE CAUSE IS KNOWN, not undetermined: `AGENT_RULES` (`validate-pipeline-artifact.mjs:93`) is keyed by bare role names, `checkArtifacts` does `AGENT_RULES[String(agentType||'').toLowerCase()]` at `:654` and `if (!rules) return { failures }` at `:656`, so a namespaced agent type returns zero failures for every agent, every artifact and every rule, before any root, mtime or active-issue resolution. Measured with the shipped hook on the #43 fixture (7 known violations), one fixture, four cells: `secops` -> block naming all seven; `SecOps` -> block; `pipeline:secops` -> SILENT; `agent-pipeline:secops` -> SILENT. Filed as #66. THEREFORE the sentence this change ships must read, in force: THE REFUSAL IS PROVEN WHERE THE PIPELINE RUNS FROM LOCAL AGENT FILES WITH BARE AGENT NAMES, AND HAS NEVER BEEN OBSERVED WHERE IT RUNS FROM THE INSTALLED PLUGIN - WHICH IS THE SHIPPING PRODUCT AND THE DEFAULT DEPLOYMENT, AND IS THE MODE THIS CHANGE'S OWN REVIEWERS RUN IN. No sentence may scope this by repository identity, and no adopting-project reader running the plugin may be able to read it as a warranty that protects them. Every such sentence carries: the WINDOW (measured 2026-08-21), the POPULATION (one machine's ~/.claude/projects transcript corpus, 8 repositories, 1638 files), the RE-DERIVATION (count messages whose `message.content` is a plain string beginning `Stop hook feedback:\nPipeline artifact failed schema validation`, grouped by project directory, cross-tabulated against recorded `Task` `subagent_type` values; and run the four-cell `agent_type` fixture against the shipped hook), and its OWN EXPIRY: the correct outcome for #66 is that somebody fixes it, on which day this sentence becomes false with no event that notices, because a silence has no event. The shipped text must therefore say, in itself, that it is a dated record and point at #66 as the thing whose closure retires it. (c) THE FAIL-OPEN DEGRADATIONS of the SubagentStop path: the validator is fail-open by contract and its own `decision:block` is advisory (`validate-pipeline-artifact.mjs:44-48`), so the enforced half degrades to nothing when node is absent, when the plugin root is unset, when the active issue is unresolvable, when the artifact's mtime exceeds 30 minutes, and - dominantly, and this is the one that screens off the other four - when the stopping agent's type does not match an `AGENT_RULES` key. (d) THE EMPTY-STRING RESIDUAL, WITH ITS COUNT AND ITS SANCTIONED VALUE: the walker implements no `minLength`, so the empty string is the cheapest value that satisfies the required field, and the requirement cannot be conditioned on severity. On the deployment where the gate fires, 17 of 229 already-written vulnerability rows carry no `remediation` - info 9, low 4, medium 4, and ZERO of the 3 critical and ZERO of the 26 high - so the empty string is what a no-remediation observation row will carry, and the shipped description must say that rather than leave a reviewer to discover it. This is the cheap half of a two-halved property stated inside the change whose subject is that exact failure, which is why it is disclosed rather than glossed. (e) THE ARCHIVE RESIDUAL, STATED AS THE INVARIANT THAT HOLDS UNDER BOTH REDACTOR VERSIONS AND NOT AS A SNAPSHOT OF ONE. `knowledge-store.mjs`'s archival redactor rewrites a value whose LEADING TOKEN is path-shaped, and a SecOps property statement opens with a route more often than any other role's. HOW MUCH of the value is rewritten is a live moving part and must not be asserted as shipped fact: at `origin/main` today `ABSOLUTE_VALUE = /^(?:\/|[A-Za-z]:[\\/])/` replaces the WHOLE value, so '/v1/public-feed must be unreachable without a server-validated bearer token' archives as the bare marker and the security claim is destroyed; on the unmerged sibling branch `fix/lane2-durable-record` (commit `b279ffa`, 'Closes #59') `LEADING_SPAN = /^(?:\/|[A-Za-z]:[\\/])[^\s"']*/ ` replaces only the leading span, and the same value archives as '<redacted-absolute-path> must be unreachable without a server-validated bearer token' with the claim intact. WHICHEVER OF THE TWO MERGES SECOND FALSIFIES THE OTHER'S SHIPPED CLAIM, and neither a schema `description` field nor an issue comment is covered by any test that would catch the staleness. So the shipped text states only what is true under both: a property statement that OPENS with a route reaches the archived reader with that opening token replaced by a marker; whether the remainder survives depends on the redactor version in force; and the reader is told the one-line check (`grep -n 'ABSOLUTE_VALUE\|LEADING_SPAN' plugins/pipeline/scripts/knowledge-store.mjs`) that tells them which version they have. #59 owns the mechanism and this change does not re-file it; the disclosure is the ask. The set of residuals is derived from every transform the field passes through between the reviewer's write and the archived read, not from the two the first draft happened to measure. (f) THE NEIGHBOUR LIMIT: the annotation must be scoped so that no reader can infer from it that the file's OTHER declared constraints are enforced. Measurably they are not: `peer-review.schema.json`'s `panelVerdict` concerns.items has no `required` list at all, 10 archived panel rows already carry severity values outside its declared enum, and the root's `required: [final_verdict, reviewed_at]` has no validation path whatsoever because every AGENT_RULES entry for that file points at `#/definitions/panelVerdict` and never at `#`. Do not describe a nag as a gate, and do not let an honesty annotation about one field warrant its neighbours.

R6. Put the rule and its force in the SAME passage, in every file the rule appears in. A reviewer reads its agent contract; it does not open `review.schema.json`. So wherever R1's sentence is STATED as binding, the same passage says what refuses a violation and what does not - which for the ten files AC1 counts means naming the Phase 2 block, the Phase 4 non-block, and the deployment-mode-scoped record from R5(b) with its date and its pointer to #66. No reader may acquire the obligation without acquiring its force at the same time, and no reader running the installed plugin may acquire a force claim that is false for them.

R7. Reconcile the SecOps contract, with the EDIT SCOPE and the ASSERTION SCOPE stated as the same set of lines. R7 edits exactly three sites: `secops.md:29` ("be specific about the remediation"), the `secops.md:169` example (which names a middleware and a rate limit), and the `secops.md:192` VETO reply template - plus the `vulnerabilities[].remediation` description in `review.schema.json`. It edits NOTHING else in `secops.md`. Line citations are re-pinned at the merge base before use (R11). The criterion that checks it must distinguish the three speech acts a security contract contains, because a whole-file sweep for 'prose naming a mechanism' hits eight lines and strips seven that must survive: (i) a FINDING ABOUT A DIFF is bound by R1; (ii) an INSPECTION PROMPT the reviewer addresses to itself - `secops.md:52,55,65,73,84,85`, what to look FOR - is not a finding and is not bound; (iii) a PRE-CODE DIRECTIVE injected into an implementer's prompt - `secops.md:107`, inside the standard-tier constraints block the orchestrator copies verbatim into the Dev thread IN PLACE OF a Phase 2 review - is protected on R8's footing. The VETO must remain actionable: a veto that says only "this is insecure" is still useless, and R1(b)'s named observation is what makes the property form actionable rather than weaker. The replacement for the `:169` example must satisfy R2(c): at least one shipped example in the SecOps contract exhibits an externally-fixed IDENTIFIER, not only an externally-fixed number.

R8. Preserve, unchanged in force, the two licences this rule routes solution design INTO and the one baseline it must not strip. (a) QA's and Dev's mechanism licence: `qa.md:181` ("Suggest: extract pure function, inject dependency, split side effect") and `qa.md:184` ("You name the problem and the fix; you do not write the fix") are the TDD handoff, not an instance of the behaviour the rule stops. (b) The SecOps standard-tier constraints block (`secops.md:107` and its surrounding block), which is the one place a REVIEWER role is contractually required to issue imperatives to an implementer, and which at the standard tier is the ONLY security review the change gets. After this change that block must constrain an implementer at least as tightly as it does at HEAD. Any edit touching either must be shown to preserve or widen it.

R9. FOLD IN the slash-command placeholder defect at `commands/pipeline.md:646-648` AND `:842-844`, both definitions (see out_of_scope for the boundary reasoning and open_questions q4/q5 for the rulings). The property: the `surface_probe` definition must, under BOTH of its readings - the raw file as `test-panel-composition-fail-direction.sh:73` extracts and executes it, and the command text as the slash-command loader renders it - pass the module basename and the predicate export name as the probe's two arguments. Neither reading may deliver the issue number, a literal `$1`, or an empty string. The two definitions stay byte-identical, as `commands/pipeline.md:838-840` instructs and `test-panel-composition-fail-direction.sh:68-73` asserts, which is why this is both-or-neither rather than a judgement call. Do not prescribe the mechanism; QA and Dev own that choice, and at least one satisfying mechanism exists inside the owned files (verified as an existence proof, NOT a mandate).

R10. Write the deferrals into ALREADY-OPEN issues before this PR merges, each with its measured evidence rather than as a claim that it was routed. The implementation opens NO new issue; the one new issue this ask produced (#66) was opened at spec time under explicit orchestrator authorization and its body already carries the full record. (a) #38 gains the Phase-4-required half: the three self-test case names that redden and the file they live in. (b) #38 ALSO gains a cross-reference to #66 stating what has moved out of #38's scope: the enforcement-escape record, now diagnosed, lives in #66; what remains #38's is the typed-provenance-and-admissibility question. The #66 body carries the 17 archived violations, the deployment-mode 2x2 with its snapshot date, the four-cell `agent_type` fixture, the three screened-off candidate causes, and the one link nobody observed. (c) #52 gains the name of every free-text field this change ADDS to the committed-and-archived-verbatim surface - which is TWO fields, not one, because R3(b) makes `vulnerabilities[].remediation` compulsory - so its eventual fix is built against the current field set rather than a stale enumeration. (d) #59 gains the interaction, stated CONDITIONALLY and not as a snapshot: after this change the redactor acts on the binding statement of a security blocker on a field the schema makes REQUIRED, and how much of that statement survives depends on which redactor version is in force - `ABSOLUTE_VALUE` at `origin/main` destroys the whole value, `LEADING_SPAN` on `fix/lane2-durable-record` b279ffa preserves everything after the leading path token. The comment must name b279ffa so that whichever branch merges second, the comment is still true. Phase 4 verifies (a)-(d) by running `gh issue view <n> --comments` itself; an impl report asserting the routing does not satisfy R10.

R11. RE-PIN EVERY MEASUREMENT AND LINE CITATION AT THE MERGE BASE BEFORE CITING IT. The spec was measured against worktree HEAD `3b87a98`; `origin/main` is `a5a9a4e`, three commits ahead (#47 `328baa5`, #37 `f28e40c`, #33 `a5a9a4e`), and the orchestrator rebases before Phase 3. What is CONFIRMED unaffected, verified by SecOps and DevOps independently with `git diff --name-only`: `agents/`, `commands/`, `schemas/` and `evidence.md` are byte-identical between the two, so all ten `secops.md` citations, `art-director.md:52-54` and `knowledge-store.mjs:136/:142-148` still land on the quoted text. What IS affected and must be re-derived rather than copied: (i) `bash plugins/pipeline/tests/run.sh` green, because the suite gained `test-moving-ref-population.sh`, `test-harness.sh` and a rewritten `test-claims-consumers.sh`; (ii) the `test-panel-composition-fail-direction.sh:645-656` citation in measured_state, which has shifted to approximately `:644` because #47 removed 2 net lines above it (its siblings `:68-73` and `:73` are unaffected and were re-verified). `git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main` at implementation time is the check: non-zero means the suite-green and line-number claims are owed a re-measure before they are cited.
acceptance_criteria: AC1. The canonical rule sentence appears in the shared Phase 4 preamble in `commands/pipeline.md` and in all nine files under `plugins/pipeline/agents/`, and in each of those ten files it carries ALL THREE of R1's clauses: scope (what-must-be-true vs how), measurability (the property names the observation that decides it, makeable by someone other than its author), and halves (a two-halved property says in itself that satisfying the cheap half approves the defect). A count below ten fails; so does a tenth file carrying clause (a) alone.

AC2. The same passage names BOTH colliding rules explicitly - the guardrail-refuses rule and the evidence.md ship-or-block line - and states that each stays allowed and WHY (cost of a property; reachability of a defect). A passage that asserts they coexist without saying why fails: the issue asked for the reconciliation, not a promise of one.

AC3. THE DISCRIMINATOR IS DECIDABLE FROM THE WRITTEN ASK ALONE, BY A READER WHO DID NOT WRITE IT. Both of R2's exemptions are stated, and the criterion is checked by handing a second reader the shipped passage and FIVE asks, requiring the passage to classify all five the same way for both readers: (1) 'the rate limit must be low enough that credential stuffing is not economical, measured by <observation>' -> IN BOUNDS; (2) 'the token lifetime must be short enough that a leaked token expires before a human can act on it, measured by <observation>' -> IN BOUNDS; (3) 'the failed-login lockout threshold must be at most 6 attempts, per the applicable card-data standard' -> IN BOUNDS (literal with a named source); (4) 'the webhook signature must be verified with the provider's HMAC-SHA256 scheme' -> IN BOUNDS (externally-fixed IDENTIFIER, which is the class round 1's illustrations omitted); (5) 'the retry budget must be at most 3' with no source named -> OUT OF BOUNDS. If two readers can differ on any of the five, the criterion fails. TWO FAILURE MODES ARE NAMED AND BOTH FAIL THE CRITERION. Under-refusing: a passage that discriminates by listing forbidden vocabulary (middleware, library, numeric limit, code shape) fails, because it refuses (3) and (4) while admitting a dressed-up reviewer literal. OVER-REFUSING, which is round 1's error and which SecOps attributed to its own wording: a passage that attaches 'however abstractly it is phrased' to the bound's ORIGIN fails, because it refuses (1) and (2) - the canonical property form for the majority of security findings, which no statute backs - and a reviewer with that reading has silence as its only in-bounds option. The passage must also name the non-binding field a candidate mechanism lands in, and at least one shipped example must be an IDENTIFIER rather than a number.

AC4. THE LOCATION MATRIX, AND IT IS THE CRITERION THAT ACTUALLY EXERCISES THE NEW FIELD AND THE ONE THAT CHECKS R5(a)'s COMPLETENESS. Run the shipped `hooks/subagent-stop.sh` against fixtures covering {role in dba, secops} x {finding location in concerns[], vulnerabilities[], compliance_flags[]} x {property field absent, non-empty, empty string}. Required outcomes on the two GUARDED locations: absent -> `decision:block` naming the field; non-empty -> silent, exit 0; empty string -> silent (the empty-string residual is real and must be demonstrated, not assumed). Required outcome on the UNGUARDED third location: `{verdict: VETO, concerns: [], vulnerabilities: [], compliance_flags: [{}]}` -> SILENT, exit 0, both before and after the change - AND the shipped honesty statement must PREDICT that silence. The criterion is the agreement between the statement's prediction and the observed outcome IN ALL THREE CHANNELS; a statement that enumerates two guarded channels and omits the third fails even though every guarded cell passes. At least one cell places the finding OUTSIDE `concerns[]`: a critical auth-bypass in `vulnerabilities[]` with `concerns: []`, which is the shape `secops.md:156-171` tells SecOps to write, must BLOCK. NON-ZERO CONTROL, required: every blocking cell must be shown SILENT under the unmutated plugin, so the block is attributable to the schema change. ENVIRONMENT NOTE, load-bearing per #66: every cell must be run with a BARE `agent_type`, because a namespaced one returns zero failures unconditionally and would make the whole matrix silent - a matrix run under a namespaced agent type is a zero result about the harness, not about the schema.

AC5. `node plugins/pipeline/scripts/validate-pipeline-artifact.mjs --self-test` still reports `0 failed` and at least 68 passed, and `bash plugins/pipeline/tests/run.sh` is green AT THE REBASED MERGE BASE, not at the round-2 base: `git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main` must be 0 when the green is recorded, because the suite gained three files since the spec's measurement (R11). THE GREEN IS A NON-REGRESSION SIGNAL, NOT COVERAGE, and the criterion says so where it is read: the self-test builds every review agentBlock with `concerns: []` (`validate-pipeline-artifact.mjs:781, :998`), so it never reaches the concern-item subschema and its result is IDENTICAL before and after the change. AC4 is the criterion that exercises the field; an implementation report citing 68/0 as evidence that the field works has misread this criterion. The discriminator is dispatch form, and the cause is the AGENT_RULES lookup miss at :654-656, which I re-derived independently with the four-cell fixture. AC7 now carries a mechanical prohibition on the repository-scoped wording, and the round-2 sentence is the SECOND mutation in AC7's table - a control with a live subject rather than a planted one. Recorded because it is uncomfortable and instructive: my own round-2 out_of_scope named the payload's agent_type as an untested candidate and then ruled the cause undetermined in the same breath. The answer was in my own list of things I had not looked at. (2) #66 IS FILED. The defect is live, severe and cross-project, and its fix touches a file owned by no session and a test owned by another active one, and would begin enforcing on other sessions' in-flight runs. It is stated as properties, not as a mechanism, per the very rule this issue introduces - including the load-bearing one: a lookup miss and a clean artifact must not produce byte-identical output. q6's round-2 ruling is marked SUPERSEDED rather than quietly edited, and the counter-argument I recorded against my own recommendation there is the one that turned out to be decisive. Naming it as unreached costs nothing and is what was asked; guarding it is explicitly out of scope. AC4 gains a compliance column whose assertion is the STATEMENT'S PREDICTION matching the observed silence, so a fourth location added later is visibly missing. (4) THE PROVENANCE DISCRIMINATOR IS MOVED FROM THE BOUND'S ORIGIN TO THE ASK'S FORM. SecOps supplied the round-1 wording, watched it implemented faithfully, and withdrew it: 'a value the reviewer chose is out of bounds however abstractly it is phrased' has a reading that refuses the canonical property form for the majority of security findings, leaving a reviewer with silence as its only in-bounds option. R5(d) carries the count and the split. (7) THE REDACTOR CLAIM IS MADE MERGE-ORDER-PROOF. DevOps found an unmerged sibling branch that already narrows the redaction to the leading span, and verified on this spec's own cited example that the security claim survives it. R5(e) now asserts only the invariant that holds under both versions and hands the reader the one-line check for which they have; R10(d)'s #59 comment must name b279ffa; and AC15 moved OUT of the unmutable list because its comment-CONTENT half is assertable even though its tracker-write half is not. WHAT COULD NOT BE FULLY RESOLVED INSIDE THE BOUNDARY, stated rather than papered over: the compliance channel stays unguarded (named, not fixed); the Phase 4 panel half stays unenforced (#38); the validator stays inert in plugin installs for the duration of this change (#66); and the gate this change ships will therefore not fire for the reviewers of this change. concerns.description: THE 56-VERSUS-0 SPLIT IS DRAWN ON THE WRONG AXIS, AND THE CAUSE IS NOT UNDETERMINED. I re-derived the census independently and BA's numbers are exactly right: 56 genuine hook-delivered blocks, 0 in any agent-pipeline project directory, besidecare-mono 52 / besidecare-public-website 4. I also confirmed BA's warning about the filter and went one step further than the string-prefix guard: I classified EVERY line in every agent-pipeline transcript containing the substring (38 of them) by content shape, and all 38 are tool_result echoes, tool_use inputs or assistant-text quotations - none is a delivered hook message in any shape, so the 0 is robust to the array-content form too, not only to the prefix filter. WHAT FALSIFIES THE SPEC: the split is not adopting-project-versus-this-repository. Blocks by repo, against pipeline-agent dispatch form (bare `secops` versus plugin-namespaced `pipeline:secops`, read from the recorded Task tool_use inputs): besidecare-mono 709 bare / 0 namespaced / 52 blocks; besidecare-public-website 24 bare / 8 namespaced / 4 blocks; nsmedia-platform 0 bare / 362 namespaced / 0 blocks; tether 9 / 81 / 0; rome 0 / 33 / 0; agent-pipeline 0 / 123 / 0; nsmedia-public-website 0 / 15 / 0; brown-dog-bites-public 0 / 8 / 0. All 56 blocks sit in the two repositories that dispatch BARE. Six repositories and 622 namespaced dispatches produced zero blocks - including nsmedia-platform, which is an ADOPTING project with 362 pipeline agent dispatches and no block ever. At besidecare-mono's observed rate (52/709 = 7.3%) that cell should hold roughly 26. So R5(b)'s sentence 'PROVEN in adopting projects and NEVER observed in this repository' is false in both halves as a description of the measured population, and an adopting-project reader running the plugin will read it as a warranty that does not hold for them. THE STRUCTURAL REASON FOR THE SPLIT, verified on disk rather than inferred: besidecare-mono carries local .claude/agents/{ba,dba,secops,...}.md, a local .claude/hooks/subagent-stop.sh invoking $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/scripts/validate-pipeline-artifact.mjs, and .claude/settings.json enabledPlugins {'pipeline@agent-pipeline': false} - the plugin is DISABLED there. besidecare-public-website has the same local-agents layout. agent-pipeline has no .claude/agents at all; nsmedia-platform's holds only ads-analyst.md. Local agent file -> bare agent name; plugin agent -> namespaced name. THE MECHANISM, measured with the SHIPPED hook against the #43 archived SecOps shard (7 known missing `description` fields), four cells, same fixture, same scratch project root: agent_type 'secops' -> decision:block naming all seven (POSITIVE CONTROL); 'SecOps' -> block (the lowercase normalisation works); 'pipeline:secops' -> SILENT, empty stdout; 'agent-pipeline:secops' -> SILENT. Cause: AGENT_RULES (validate-pipeline-artifact.mjs:93) is keyed by bare role names only, and checkArtifacts does `AGENT_RULES[String(agentType||'').toLowerCase()]` at :654 then `if (!rules) return { failures }` at :656. A namespaced agent_type therefore returns zero failures for EVERY agent, EVERY artifact, EVERY rule - before pipelineDirs, before activeIssueDir, before the RECENT_MS mtime test. That ordering is itself corroboration: it explains why all three of BA's candidates measured 'did not occur' AND why the silence is total rather than intermittent - with the lookup missing, none of those three code paths is ever reached. THE ONE LINK I DID NOT OBSERVE, stated plainly: I did not directly observe the SubagentStop payload's agent_type string, only the Task tool's subagent_type. The observation that decides it, makeable by anyone in one run: register a SubagentStop hook that appends its stdin to a file, dispatch any pipeline agent in a project whose agents come from the plugin, and read the recorded agent_type. Note the spec ALREADY names this exact host behaviour as an untested candidate in out_of_scope ('what agent_type the SubagentStop payload carries for a plugin-scoped agent') and then rules the cause undetermined anyway. Even if that link were to fail, the 2x2 above falsifies R5(b)'s scoping on its own, without any mechanism. WHY THIS CLOSES NOW RATHER THAN BEING FILED: AC15 routes this record into #38 as the evidence a future fix is to be built against. A wrong number replaced by another wrong number is the same defect living inside its own fix; if #38 is seeded with a repository-scoped split it will be built against the wrong discriminator. WHAT A CORRECT FIX MUST SATISFY: (i) every sentence this change writes about who refuses a non-conforming concern is scoped by the DEPLOYMENT MODE under which the refusal was observed, not by repository identity, so that a reader in an adopting project running the plugin cannot conclude the gate protects them; (ii) the record routed to #38 carries the discriminator that actually separates the 56 from the 0, together with the cell that falsifies the repository framing (an adopting project, plugin-installed, hundreds of dispatches, zero blocks); (iii) where a cause is stated as undetermined, the candidates that were tested are listed WITH the one that was named and not tested, so the next reader does not re-derive it. MEASURABLE BY: re-running the per-repository 2x2 (dispatch form x blocks) over ~/.claude/projects with the string-prefix filter, and the four-cell agent_type fixture against the shipped hook. Both are re-derivable by a reader other than me and both can fail.

THE SECOND NOT-NULL COLUMN'S 'ZERO IMPACT' IS A ZERO OVER AN EMPTY POPULATION - the same defect I raised in round 1, recurring one table over. BA's figure is arithmetically correct and I reproduced it exactly (17 -> 30 archived errors, 13 new, 0 attributable to the vulnerabilities requirement; identical whether vulnerabilities.items.required is [severity, description, remediation] or [remediation] alone). But the reason it is 0 is that the archived Phase 2 population contains NO vulnerability rows at all: 43.json .review.secops carries `vulnerabilities: []`, and the only archived array with content (34.json .peer-review.secops, 1 row) is validated against peer-review.schema.json #/definitions/panelVerdict, which declares no vulnerabilities property, so R3(b) cannot reach it. A zero measured over an empty population says nothing about the requirement. THE POPULATION THAT DECIDES IT is the deployment where the gate actually fires, and it is not empty. Counted across besidecare-mono and besidecare-public-website .pipeline artifacts (review*.json and peer-review*.json): 224 already-written vulnerability rows, of which 17 carry no `remediation` - by severity: info 9, low 4, medium 4, and ZERO of the 3 critical and ZERO of the 26 high rows. Not one row anywhere carries an empty-string remediation today. Two things follow. First, the requirement costs nothing where R3(b)'s own rationale applies (blocking findings: 29/29 conformant), and everything it does cost falls on non-blocking observation rows where 'there is nothing to remediate' is a legitimate state. Second, R3 states the scope as 'MACHINE-REQUIRED at every LOCATION a Phase 2 BLOCKING finding can occupy', but the mechanism cannot condition on severity - the walker implements type, enum, required, minItems, items and allOf only (validate-pipeline-artifact.mjs:201-229; no if/then, no minLength), which out_of_scope concedes - so the requirement necessarily widens from 'blocking findings' to 'all rows'. Combined with R5(d), the sanctioned value for those 17 rows is the empty string, which is the cheap half of a two-halved property, in the change whose subject is that exact failure. WHAT A CORRECT FIX MUST SATISFY: any claim this change makes about what the vulnerabilities requirement costs already-written rows must name the population it counted, and that population must be one in which the constraint can actually fire; and where the requirement is broader than the rationale that justifies it (all severities, not blocking ones), the schema description and R5's residual list must say so, say that the empty string is what a no-remediation row will carry, and carry the count. MEASURABLE BY: for the deployment the claim is about, count vulnerability rows by severity with and without the field, in artifacts already on disk. A count of 0 must be shown to come from a non-empty population.

THE REVERSIBILITY GUARD WAS NOT WIDENED TO THE SUBSCHEMA THIS ROUND ADDED. R4 forbids additionalProperties:false on 'either concern-item subschema' and AC10 asserts the down direction over review.schema.json #/definitions/agentBlock, #/properties/secops and peer-review.schema.json #/definitions/panelVerdict. R3(b) now edits a THIRD subschema - #/properties/secops's vulnerabilities.items - giving a required list to a subschema that previously had none. That is the subschema an editor's hands are on this round, and it is the one the forbidden-edit rule does not name. The exposure is small but real and I measured it rather than assuming: of 253 already-written vulnerability rows across besidecare, agent-pipeline and the archive, 1 carries undeclared keys (`resolved`, `resolution`), so closing that subschema would strand it. Note that AC10's down-direction check as phrased would still pass: it validates a NEW-contract shard against the pre-change schemas, and a shard whose vulnerabilities rows carry only declared keys is silent about the property. WHAT A CORRECT FIX MUST SATISFY: the forbidden-edit rule and the down-direction assertion must cover every item subschema this change gives a required list to, not only the two the round-1 review happened to name. The invariant is unchanged: an instance valid under either contract version remains valid under the other. MEASURABLE BY: apply additionalProperties:false to each edited item subschema in turn and re-run the archived-and-live replay; each must redden, and a subschema for which no mutation exists is a subschema the guard does not cover.

The expected-survivor slot names a CRITERION rather than a surviving MUTATION. The entry's reasoning is sound and its re-anchor condition is written into the criterion, which is the part that matters. But every other row in the table pairs a criterion with a mutation and a predicted colour, and AC5's two listed mutations are both expected to REDDEN, so the table as written contains no mutation predicted to survive. The surviving mutation is available and already measured: AC4's first mutation (remove the new field from review.schema.json's agentBlock required list) leaves AC5 at 68 passed / 0 failed. WHAT A CORRECT FIX MUST SATISFY: the documented survivor is a named mutation with a predicted outcome of SURVIVES, so that the slot can be checked by running something rather than by agreeing with a paragraph.

concerns.description: THE PROVENANCE DISCRIMINATOR TESTS THE AUTHOR'S MENTAL HISTORY, WHICH NO READER CAN OBSERVE, AND ON THE AVAILABLE READING IT REFUSES THE CANONICAL PROPERTY FORM. This is my round-1 wording, implemented faithfully, and it is wrong in one direction; the attribution is mine. R2(b): 'a value the reviewer chose is out of bounds however abstractly it is phrased.' AC3: 'a threshold the reviewer picked itself is out of bounds however abstractly phrased.' Both sentences take as their subject the bound's ORIGIN and then quantify over every phrasing of it, which admits two readings. (i) NARROW: forbids binding on a literal the reviewer picked while dressing it in abstract clothes. Correct, and surely intended. (ii) BROAD: forbids any bound originating in the reviewer's judgement, however phrased. Reading (ii) refuses 'the rate limit must be low enough that credential stuffing is not economical', 'the payload cap must be small enough that one request cannot exhaust the parser', 'the token lifetime must be short enough that a leaked token expires before a human can act on it' - the canonical R1-conformant form for the three most common SecOps asks that no statute backs, i.e. the large majority of security findings. The mechanism is that provenance-of-a-LITERAL is observable in the artifact (a source is named or it is not) while provenance-of-a-JUDGEMENT is observable nowhere, so a criterion resting on the latter cannot be applied by anyone but the author - which is exactly what R1(b) forbids. evidence.md:273-276 is the applicable line: 'A gate that blocks correct work gets switched off by the operator, which costs more than having no gate ... Check both directions before trusting one.' SECOND, SMALLER, SAME CLAUSE: R2(b)'s illustration set ('a regulation's threshold, an interop contract's version floor, a named advisory's fixed version') is three NUMERIC forms, and AC3's one worked example is also a number, while the externally-fixed values SecOps states most often are IDENTIFIERS - a provider's HMAC-SHA256 webhook scheme, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, PKCE `S256`. The general clause ('a value an authority OUTSIDE this reviewer fixed') covers them; the illustrations do not exhibit them; and q3's own resolution rules that the shipped EXAMPLE is what a reviewer copies. SEVERITY REASONING, stated because it is not obvious: both halves fail in the OVER-REFUSING direction, and evidence.md section 7 says over-refusing 'can be filed, with the cost stated'. I am applying that literally rather than escalating, and the cost is stated: until it is fixed, a SecOps reviewer has an available reading under which the only in-bounds form of a non-statutory bound is silence, and the rule is about to be replicated into ten files.

A bound that appears in the ask only as a stated condition with a named observation is in bounds whoever first thought of it. concerns.description: THE NEVER-OBSERVED CLAIM SHIPS AS A PRESENT-TENSE UNIVERSAL WITH NO WINDOW, INTO TEN FILES, WITH NO WAY FOR A LATER READER TO TELL WHETHER IT IS STILL TRUE. The correct outcome for the escape is that somebody fixes it, and on the day they do, twelve files assert something false with no mechanism that notices, because a silence has no event. It failed loudly only because its author wrote the expiry into the assertion message') applied to a prose claim rather than an assertion. concerns.description: Performed the AC3 two-reader classification myself (the human judgement the panel was told to render). Asks (1),(2),(3),(5) classify unambiguously against the shipped canonical block text: (1) and (3) appear near-verbatim as the passage's own worked IN-BOUNDS examples; (5) matches the passage's own worked OUT-BOUNDS example almost verbatim; (2) is structurally identical in shape to the rate-limit worked example (a bound stated as a condition plus 'measured by <observation>', no literal number), so it classifies the same way by the same test. Ask (4) - 'the webhook signature must be verified with the provider's HMAC-SHA256 scheme', the externally-fixed IDENTIFIER case R2(c) and AC3 both flag as the class round 1's illustrations omitted - is where two readers can genuinely diverge. Every worked example the shipped passage actually carries for the 'externally-fixed value, source named' exemption includes an explicit 'per <X>' citation ('per the applicable card-data standard'; 'per the provider's webhook docs'). Ask (4) as literally worded in AC3 carries no 'per X' citation - it says only 'the provider's HMAC-SHA256 scheme'. A strict reader applying the passage's own stated test verbatim ('is a checkable source for that literal named?') can reasonably answer NO on ask (4) - 'the provider's' names an owner, not a citable document - while a reader reasoning by class (HMAC-SHA256 is itself a self-identifying externally-fixed standard name) answers YES. Both readings are defensible from the shipped text alone; the passage does not resolve which one governs, because its own two illustrations model a citation the tested ask omits.
concerns.property_a_correct_fix_must_satisfy: Every worked example the shipped passage carries for the externally-fixed-value exemption must exhibit a form that matches at least one of AC3's five test asks closely enough that a reader applying the passage's own stated test to that ask reaches only one answer. Concretely: either AC3's ask (4) needs a citation clause matching the shipped illustrations' shape, or the shipped illustrations need a bare, uncited identifier form (so the passage itself demonstrates that a self-identifying standard name is a sufficient source without a 'per X' clause). Currently neither is true, so the criterion whose whole point is decidability-from-the-ask-alone has a live case where two readers can disagree.

deploy_notes: This PR changes commands/pipeline.md and agents/*.md, which Claude Code loads from the INSTALLED PLUGIN CACHE (<redacted-absolute-path> at slash-command invocation time, not from the repo checkout. Confirmed directly: cache commands/pipeline.md has 2 occurrences of the pre-fix '"$1" "$2"' surface_probe form and 0 of the post-fix '"${1}" "${2}"' form; the worktree at HEAD has the reverse (0 / 2). Merging this PR to origin/main does not touch that cache file, and nothing in the repo or in Claude Code re-syncs it automatically on merge.

The repo's OWN established convention for exactly this class of change is plugins/pipeline/README.md's '### Upgrading' section (line 72): a numbered, dated changelog of 'changes in this release [that] alter BEHAVIOUR on an existing project at its next plugin update, with no action on your part', currently enumerating twelve items (e.g. item 11's absolute-path redaction, item 9's phase-entry-guard abstention). That section already states, as house style, that behaviour changes here take effect only 'at its next plugin update' -- i.e. the project already has language for the merge-vs-runtime gap. This PR's own Dev-initiated fold-in F1 (the surface_probe "$1"->"${1}" fix in commands/pipeline.md, which is the entire subject of AC9.brace/AC12/AC13/AC14) is exactly this class of change and is NOT added as a thirteenth entry: `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` does not include README.md at all. So the specific mechanism this repo uses to tell an operator 'this fix is not live until you update the plugin' was available, applicable, and not used for the one behavioural fix in this diff that most needs it.

Deploy-order consequence, stated as a property: after this PR merges, origin/main and any PR/issue commentary correctly claim the AC12/AC9.brace fix shipped, while every real /pipeline invocation in every installed-plugin deployment (which this same spec's R5(b) establishes is the DEFAULT and dominant deployment mode, ahead of local-agent-file deployments) continues to execute the broken "$1" "$2" form until that installation's plugin cache is separately refreshed. The window has no announced start (no README entry), no observable end (no version check, no cache-vs-source drift assertion, and no CI or hook runs in the installed-plugin runtime environment at all, so nobody is notified when the window closes), and no documented remediation step for an adopting project (the only written remediation found anywhere accessible to this review is a PERSONAL memory note about this developer's own machine, not a repository artifact any adopting-project operator would see).

Distinct and lower severity: within the repo's own CI/test boundary there is no deploy-order hazard from this specific point, because run.sh and validate-pipeline-artifact.mjs read the worktree copies directly, never the plugin cache. The hazard is confined to the slash-command/agent-dispatch runtime path (a live operator session), not to CI.

concerns.direction: Residual: RFC 6238 could acquire an erratum or be obsoleted and none of the thirteen copies would notice. Materially smaller shelf-life risk than evidence.md's 'control anchored to a live defect'.
